512.title: The good shepherd (John 10:1–18)
512.hook: he knows his sheep by name and they know his voice
512.howItsDone: On the fourth Sunday of Easter, Good Shepherd Sunday, Catholics hear a reading from John 10 at Mass, and the Church prays that day for vocations to the priesthood and religious life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the healed man stood his ground: one thing I know. Your line was now I see. What did you notice that you hadn't seen before? Day five hundred twelve.

In a crowded airport, a hundred voices blur into noise. Then someone, far off, says your name, and your head turns before you've decided anything. Your name cuts through. Travelers in the Middle East have described something like it with sheep: several flocks sheltering together overnight, all mixed up, and in the morning each shepherd simply calls, and his own sheep sort themselves out and follow him. The man born blind has just been thrown out of the synagogue. And Jesus, right after, starts talking about sheep, voices and names.
screen: `YOUR NAME IN A CROWDED AIRPORT.` → `MIXED FLOCKS, ONE CALL.` → `RIGHT AFTER THE BLIND MAN.`

segments.voice: Jesus sets the scene: a sheepfold, a wall, a gate, a keeper at the gate. A thief climbs over the wall. The shepherd comes in by the door, and the Douay-Rheims says: "the sheep hear his voice: and he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out." Notice the order. Name first, then leading. He doesn't drive them from behind with a stick. He walks ahead and they follow a voice they know. Then comes another great I am. "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd giveth his life for his sheep." He compares a hired hand, who sees the wolf coming and runs, because the sheep aren't his. The good shepherd stays, and more than stays. The word John uses for good, kalos, also carries the sense of beautiful, noble, the real thing. And then a line about outsiders: other sheep I have, that are not of this fold; them also I must bring. Whatever else that means, the flock is bigger than the people standing there. And look where John sets this speech. A man has just been pushed out of his community for telling the truth, and Jesus goes looking for him. The shepherd keeps the one who was thrown out. Christians loved this picture early. Some of the oldest Christian paintings, on the walls of the Roman catacombs, show a young shepherd with a lamb across his shoulders. In the Catholic calendar, the fourth Sunday of Easter is called Good Shepherd Sunday, and the Church prays that day for vocations, for people called to shepherd others.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen. Sit comfortably and let the sounds around you come in: traffic, a fan, a bird, your own breath. Don't chase any of them. Then, under all the noise, imagine your own first name being said once, quietly, by someone who means you well. Let it land. If you pray, you can hold the line, he calleth his own sheep by name, and listen for his voice in the quiet. If you don't, just rest in the feeling of being known by name. The bell holds the time.
Kalos. The Greek word for good that also means noble, beautiful: what Jesus calls the shepherd who calls his own by name and lays down his life for them. Today's word.
Your line: he knows my name. Today, use someone's name when you thank them, the cashier, the driver, a coworker. Watch what it does. Day five hundred twelve.

513.title: I am the resurrection (John 11:17–27)
513.hook: grieving Martha makes a great confession of faith
513.tomorrow: The house filled with the odor
513.howItsDone: John 11 is among the Gospel readings the Church provides for funeral Masses, and Catholics pray for their dead by name, especially in November and on the anniversary of a death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kalos, the good shepherd who calls his own by name. Your line was he knows my name. Whose name did you say on purpose? Day five hundred thirteen.

At hospital bedsides and after funerals, one sentence keeps coming back. If only. If only the ambulance had come sooner. If only I'd called. If only you'd been here. It isn't really a question, and it isn't quite blame. It's love with nowhere to go. In Bethany, a village near Jerusalem, a man named Lazarus has died, and his sister Martha hears that Jesus is finally on the road. She doesn't wait at the house. She goes out to meet him, and the first thing she says is that sentence.
screen: `IF ONLY.` → `LAZARUS IS DEAD.` → `MARTHA GOES OUT TO MEET HIM.`

segments.voice: John says Lazarus has already been in the tomb four days. Friends have come from Jerusalem to comfort the sisters. Mary stays sitting in the house. Martha gets up and goes. And she says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Then, in the same breath, she adds that even now she knows God will give him whatever he asks. Grief and trust, side by side, in one speech. Jesus tells her, your brother will rise again. She answers like a believer of her time: I know he will rise again at the resurrection on the last day. True, but far off. And then Jesus pulls the far-off thing into the present tense: "I am the resurrection and the life: he that believeth in me, although he be dead, shall live." Not, I will bring the resurrection someday. I am it, standing here. He asks her straight out: believest thou this? And Martha, still grieving, answers with a full confession of faith. She says, yea, Lord, I have believed that thou art Christ the Son of the living God. Some readers set it beside Peter's confession in Matthew, which uses the same titles. Here it comes from a grieving woman on the road outside her village. Martha has a reputation, from Luke, as the busy sister who asked Jesus to send Mary to help her serve. John shows her another way: the one who walks out to meet him and says who he is. The Church offers these words among the readings for funeral Masses, and now keeps one memorial for Martha, Mary and Lazarus together.
screen: `FOUR DAYS IN THE TOMB.` · `IF THOU HADST BEEN HERE.` · `NOT SOMEDAY: I AM.` · `MARTHA'S CONFESSION.` · then, large: `I AM THE RESURRECTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring to mind someone who has died. A grandparent, a friend, someone you hardly knew but think about. See their face, or their handwriting, or the chair they sat in. Let yourself feel the if only, if there is one. You don't have to fix it. Then, if you pray, you can say Martha's words for them, or Jesus's: I am the resurrection and the life. If you don't pray, simply hold their name and let it rest in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Anastasis. The Greek word for resurrection, literally a standing up again: what Jesus told Martha he was, standing right in front of her. Today's word.
Your line: love with nowhere to go. Today, if you pass a cemetery, a memorial or an old photo, pause for one breath and remember a name. Day five hundred thirteen.

514.title: The house filled with the odor (John 12:1–8)
514.hook: Mary of Bethany anoints his feet with costly nard
514.howItsDone: The Church reads the anointing at Bethany at Mass on the Monday of Holy Week.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martha on the road: anastasis. Your line was love with nowhere to go. Whose name did you remember? Day five hundred fourteen.

A scent doesn't stay politely in one corner. It fills a room, gets into curtains, follows people home on their clothes. Long after the guests have gone, a house can still smell of the dinner. Six days before the Passover, Jesus is back in Bethany at a dinner, and Lazarus, the man who was dead, is sitting at the table. Then his sister Mary opens a jar, and nobody in the house can miss what happens next.
screen: `A SCENT WON'T STAY PUT.` → `SIX DAYS BEFORE THE PASCH.` → `DINNER IN BETHANY.`

segments.voice: Martha is serving. Lazarus is at the table. And Mary takes a pound of ointment, spikenard, of great price, John says. She pours it on Jesus's feet and wipes them with her hair. Then John adds one sentence that's pure memory, as if he can still smell it. The Douay-Rheims says: "and the house was filled with the odour of the ointment." Odour is the British spelling of odor, and here it just means scent, fragrance. Judas objects. Why wasn't this sold for three hundred pence and given to the poor? A penny there is a denarius, roughly a day's pay for a laborer, so this jar is worth three hundred days of a laborer's pay, poured out in a minute. John says plainly that Judas didn't care about the poor; he kept the purse and helped himself. Jesus defends her: let her alone, she has kept it for the day of my burial. Then: "For the poor you have always with you; but me you have not always." People sometimes hear that as a shrug about poverty. Readers who know Deuteronomy hear an echo instead: the poor will not be wanting in the land, it says, and so open your hand to them. Read that way, Jesus is saying, this moment won't come again. Mary seems to understand what the others don't: he is about to die. So she does something extravagant, physical and unforgettable. And the whole house knew.
screen: `MARTHA SERVES, LAZARUS EATS.` · `A POUND OF NARD, POURED.` · `THREE HUNDRED PENCE, AND JUDAS.` · `KEPT FOR MY BURIAL.` · then, large: `THE HOUSE FILLED WITH THE ODOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan something fragrant for someone. Sit, and breathe slowly through your nose a few times. Notice what you can smell right now, even faintly. Then think of one person and one generous thing you could do for them today that they'd notice: flowers on a table, bread warming, a candle lit before they come home, a handwritten note. Let the plan become concrete. If you pray, you can offer it the way Mary offered the jar. If you don't, just hold the person in mind. The bell holds the time.
Nard. The costly perfume Mary of Bethany poured on Jesus's feet, filling the whole house with its fragrance. Today's word.
Your line: the whole house knew. Today, do your fragrant thing, and don't apologize for how generous it is. Day five hundred fourteen.

515.title: The grain of wheat (John 12:24)
515.hook: unless the grain falls and dies, it stays alone
515.howItsDone: The Church reads John 12:20–33 on the Fifth Sunday of Lent in Year B, and on the feast of Saint Lawrence, deacon and martyr.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary's jar of nard, and a house full of its scent. Your line was the whole house knew. Did you do your fragrant thing? Day five hundred fifteen.

A packet of seeds can sit in a kitchen drawer for years. Open it, and the seeds are all still there, a bit drier. Nothing has gone wrong, exactly. Nothing has happened at all. Put one in the dirt, and it stops being a seed. It splits, it disappears into roots and a stalk, and if you're lucky, a whole head of grain. Jesus is in Jerusalem now, with the Passover close, and some Greeks have come asking to see him. His answer is about a seed.
screen: `SEEDS IN A DRAWER.` → `ONE IN THE DIRT.` → `SOME GREEKS ASK TO SEE HIM.`

segments.voice: The setup matters. John says some Greeks, Gentiles in the Douay, people who had come up to worship at the feast, find Philip and say, Sir, we would see Jesus. Philip tells Andrew, and the two of them tell Jesus. Then Jesus says the hour has come. All through John, his hour has been not yet. At Cana: my hour is not yet come. Now, when outsiders arrive wanting to see him, the hour is here. And this is what he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground die, itself remaineth alone. But if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." Notice the word alone. The opposite of bearing fruit, here, isn't failure. It's staying alone, intact and unchanged. A grain that keeps itself is safe, and it's by itself forever. Jesus is talking first about his own death. Readers hear an answer to the Greeks in it: a few lines on he says, if I be lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself. Then he widens it: he that loveth his life shall lose it, and he that hateth his life in this world keepeth it unto life eternal. Some readers hear hate there as a strong Semitic way of saying, don't cling. Early Christians took the seed picture straight to the martyrs. Tertullian wrote that the blood of Christians is seed: the more they're cut down, the more they grow. Catholics also hear it in smaller deaths: a pride let go, a grudge buried, an evening given up. The grain falls, and the field comes later.
screen: `WE WOULD SEE JESUS.` · `THE HOUR HAS COME.` · `UNLESS IT DIE, IT STAYS ALONE.` · `THE BLOOD OF CHRISTIANS IS SEED.` · then, large: `THE GRAIN OF WHEAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one small thing to let fall. Sit, open your hands on your lap, and breathe. Think through today and find one small self-interest: needing to win an argument, getting the last word, the bigger slice, the credit for something. Not a big sacrifice. Something seed-sized. Picture it leaving your hands and going into the ground. If you pray, you can hold the line, if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit. If you don't, just keep your hands open and breathe. The bell holds the time.
The grain of wheat. Jesus's picture of his own death: a seed that stays alone unless it falls, and bears much fruit when it does. Today's word.
Your line: falls and bears fruit. Today, let your seed-sized thing go once, on purpose, and don't mention it to anyone. Day five hundred fifteen.

516.title: The towel, slowly (John 13:1–17)
516.hook: Peter protests, then says not only my feet but my hands and head
516.howItsDone: At the Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday, the priest may wash the feet of chosen members of the parish after the homily, while an antiphon is sung.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the grain that falls into the ground. Your line was falls and bears fruit. What did you let go of? Day five hundred sixteen.

A friend offers to carry the heavy box. No, no, I've got it. Someone picks up the check, and there's an argument at the table. A nurse reaches to help a patient sit up, and the patient flinches. For some people, being helped is harder than helping. Today John slows the story right down. For the next stretch of his Gospel he stays at one supper, on one night. It begins with a towel.
screen: `NO, NO, I'VE GOT IT.` → `HARDER THAN HELPING.` → `ONE NIGHT, ONE SUPPER.`

segments.voice: John opens chapter thirteen with a sentence that frames everything left: having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them unto the end. Then he tells it almost in slow motion, in the Douay-Rheims: "He riseth from supper, and layeth aside his garments, and having taken a towel, girded himself." He pours water into a basin and begins washing the disciples' feet. It's a servant's work. Here the teacher is on the floor. Then he reaches Peter. And Peter, never one to keep quiet, says it: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus answers: "If I wash thee not, thou shalt have no part with me." Peter swings all the way around: "Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and my head." It's almost funny, and it's very Peter. Either nothing, or everything. Jesus tells him one who has bathed only needs his feet washed. What Peter has to learn first isn't how to serve. It's how to be served, to let Jesus kneel in front of him. Only after that does Jesus say, I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you do also. At the Holy Thursday Mass of the Lord's Supper, in parishes that keep the rite, the priest sets aside his outer vestment, ties on a towel, and kneels to wash the feet of people from the parish, while the rest watch. The teacher on the floor, again, once a year.
screen: `HE LOVED THEM UNTO THE END.` · `HE TAKES A TOWEL.` · `NEVER; THEN, NOT ONLY MY FEET.` · `HOLY THURSDAY, THE BASIN.` · then, large: `THE TOWEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: practice receiving. Sit and rest your feet flat on the floor. Feel them: the weight, the tiredness, maybe the ache from today. Breathe. Now think of someone who offers to help you and whom you usually wave off. Picture saying yes to them, simply, without arguing or paying it back right away. Notice what happens in you. If you pray, you can hold Peter's line, not only my feet. If you don't, just stay with the feeling of being cared for. The bell holds the time.
The towel. Jesus ties it on at the Last Supper and washes his disciples' feet, and Peter has to learn to let him. Today's word.
Your line: not only my feet. Today, the next time someone offers to help, say yes and thank you, and nothing else. Day five hundred sixteen.

517.title: A new commandment (John 13:34–35)
517.hook: love one another as I have loved you; by this all will know
517.howItsDone: At the Holy Thursday Mass of the Lord's Supper, the Church sings antiphons during the washing of feet, traditionally including one drawn from John 13:34, "Mandatum novum," a new commandment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the towel, and Peter learning to be served. Your line was not only my feet. Did you let someone help you? Day five hundred seventeen.

How do you spot a team's fans in an airport? The jersey. A nurse? The scrubs, the clip-on badge. A soldier, a chef, a judge: there's usually something you can see. Uniforms answer the question, who are you with? Judas has just gone out into the night, John says. The door closes behind him. And Jesus, with the eleven who are left, tells them how people will be able to pick them out of a crowd. It isn't a uniform.
screen: `THE JERSEY, THE SCRUBS.` → `JUDAS GOES OUT INTO THE NIGHT.` → `NOT A UNIFORM.`

segments.voice: Here are the words, in the Douay-Rheims: "A new commandment I give unto you: That you love one another, as I have loved you, that you also love one another. By this shall all men know that you are my disciples, if you have love one for another." The first thing to ask is, what's new about it? Love of neighbor isn't new. It's already in Leviticus: thou shalt love thy friend as thyself, as the Douay renders it, and Jesus quotes it himself in the other Gospels. The new part is the measure. Not as you love yourself, but as I have loved you. And how has he loved them? An hour ago he was on his knees with a towel, washing their feet. Within a day he'll lay down his life. That's the yardstick now. The second thing is the sign. All men will know. Not by a creed recited, or a building, or a badge, but by something people can watch from outside: how these people treat each other. Around the year 200, the North African writer Tertullian reported how outsiders talked about Christians in his city: look how they love one another, they said, and how ready they are to die for each other. That's the commandment working as a sign. The Latin for commandment is mandatum, and that word gave Holy Thursday its old English name, Maundy Thursday. On that night, as the priest washes feet, the Church traditionally sings an antiphon that begins, in Latin, mandatum novum: a new commandment.
screen: `NOT NEW: LEVITICUS ALREADY SAID IT.` · `NEW: AS I HAVE LOVED YOU.` · `A SIGN OUTSIDERS CAN SEE.` · `MANDATUM: MAUNDY THURSDAY.` · then, large: `A NEW COMMANDMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one visible act of love. Sit and breathe. Bring to mind the people you'll actually see today, at home, at work, at school, in a group chat. Pick one. Now pick one thing you could do for them that someone else might notice: standing up for them in a meeting, clearing their plate, a public thank you, sitting with the person nobody sits with. Picture yourself doing it. If you pray, you can hold the line, as I have loved you. If you don't, just hold that one person. The bell holds the time.
Mandatum. The Latin for commandment, the root of Maundy Thursday: love one another as Jesus loved them, with a towel and a cross. Today's word.
Your line: by this they will know. Today, do your one visible act of love, and let it be seen. Day five hundred seventeen.

518.title: Many mansions (John 14:1–6)
518.hook: let not your heart be troubled; I am the way, the truth and the life
518.howItsDone: John 14:1–6 is one of the Gospel readings offered for Catholic funeral Masses, and the Church prays daily for the dying and the dead, especially in November.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mandatum, love as I have loved you. Your line was by this they will know. What did you do that someone could see? Day five hundred eighteen.

Arriving somewhere strange is easier when someone says, we've set up the spare room for you. Clean sheets, a towel folded on the bed, maybe a glass of water on the nightstand. The bag isn't even unpacked, and already there's a place for you. At the supper, Jesus has just told Peter that he'll deny him three times before the rooster crows. It's a hard thing to hear. And the very next thing Jesus says is about rooms.
screen: `THE SPARE ROOM, READY.` → `PETER WILL DENY HIM.` → `THEN, ROOMS.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "Let not your heart be troubled. You believe in God, believe also in me. In my Father's house there are many mansions. If not, I would have told you: because I go to prepare a place for you." Mansions sounds like marble and gated driveways. In the Douay's older English, the word just meant a dwelling, a place to stay; the Latin behind it is mansiones, lodgings. So this isn't real estate. It's: there is room for you to stay, and I'm going ahead to get it ready. Then Thomas says out loud what he doesn't understand: Lord, we don't know where you're going, so how can we know the way? And Jesus answers: "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No man cometh to the Father, but by me." Thomas asked for directions. He gets a person. And notice who Jesus said it to: frightened men, one of whom was about to deny him and all of whom, he will soon tell them, would be scattered. He doesn't wait for them to be brave first. He gives the promise while they are still afraid, and the room is ready before they are.
screen: `LET NOT YOUR HEART BE TROUBLED.` · `MANSIONS: PLACES TO STAY.` · `THOMAS ASKS THE WAY.` · `SAID TO FRIGHTENED MEN.` · then, large: `MANY MANSIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone who is afraid of dying. It might be someone sick right now, someone very old, someone grieving, or a fear you carry yourself. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Picture them in a quiet room, a light on, a chair ready. Don't try to argue the fear away. Just keep them company in your mind. If you pray, you can pray for them with Jesus's words, let not your heart be troubled. If you don't, simply hold them kindly. The bell holds the time.
